paras: The lynching of Edmund Davis was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd of about 300 men near Heath's store in Union County, North Carolina, on the morning of Monday, October 17, 1881. Davis, accused of raping the daughter of an aged white widow, was taken from the constable's guard escorting him to jail and hanged near the scene of the alleged crime. Papers in both Carolinas reported that about a third of the crowd was Black and that some of them urged that he be burned.

According to the Charlotte Observer, as reprinted by the Pickens Sentinel, Mrs. Godfrey, an aged widow, lived with her daughter and a small Black servant boy about twelve and a half miles from Monroe and one mile from the South Carolina line. Around two o'clock on Sunday morning, October 16, she heard her daughter's smothered cries and sent the boy to a Black neighbor, but the intruder escaped in the dark before a light was struck. Miss Godfrey, said to be about 35, was found choked and seriously hurt, and a stick and a wagon hammer lay on the floor.

A Black neighbor identified the stick as one carried by Edmund Davis, an ex-convict out of the penitentiary six months, who had left his house that evening for a church in Lancaster County, South Carolina.

A party of neighborhood men followed Davis and captured him around eleven o'clock Sunday morning in a cabin in Lancaster County, eight miles from the Godfrey house. Brought back to Union County, he was examined by a magistrate, named in the Anderson Intelligencer as Justice McIlwain, and Miss Godfrey could not identify him because her room had been dark. The magistrate nonetheless committed him on the evidence of the stick to a constable and a deputized guard for the trip to the Monroe jail.

On the way Davis was reported to have confessed, and when word spread a lynching party of one hundred men formed. The guard hid him, in the woods according to the Farmer and Mechanic, while the crowd searched all Sunday night. He was found about daylight, and by 8:30 a crowd of 326 men, about 100 of them Black, had gathered, including what the Observer called some of the best citizens of that part of Union County.

Davis was described as indifferent to his fate and was said to have repeated his confession and declared himself willing to be hanged. Some Black members of the crowd called for burning him, but at nine o'clock he was hanged to a tree within a mile and a half of the Godfrey house. After forty minutes the crowd, satisfied that he was dead, dispersed and left the body hanging.
No report of an inquest, an arrest of any member of the crowd or any official inquiry appears in the coverage.

The story spread from the Charlotte Observer of October 18, which the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic condensed on October 20 and the Pickens Sentinel in South Carolina reprinted in full on October 27 under the headline "Another Ravisher Lynched." The Charlotte Home and Democrat ran its own local version on October 21, calling Davis "the fiend" and closing, "We are glad his request was carried out." The Farmer and Mechanic called the case "A terrible affair" and followed it with a warning to parents about "the prevalence of rape."

A short wire datelined Asheville, October 21, appeared in the Daily Gazette under "Hanged by a Mob," with a subhead placing the lynching in Asheville, though its text named Union County. The Anderson Intelligencer's news summary of October 27 gave the plainest account, noting that the party was "of both colors." Every report presented Davis's guilt and confession as fact, though they rested on the crowd's and officers' accounts and the woman had not identified him.

The Asheville wire said Davis was captured on Wednesday and taken "yesterday," October 20, while the earlier Observer account and the Anderson Intelligencer placed the hanging on Monday, October 17. Accounts also differed on whether Davis had been jailed or was still with his guard, and on the crowd's size, 300 or 326.

reader.title: Lynching of Edmund Davis
bases: A crowd took an accused Black man from the constable's guard and hanged him to a tree near the scene of the alleged crime (A2, A3, A5).
A crowd of some 300 to 326 men hanged Davis, who was in the charge of a constable and had not been tried, for an alleged rape (A2, A4, A5); the papers call it a lynching by a mob (A3, A5).

Four separate reports agree on the capture, the seizure and the hanging (A2, A3, A4, A5); A1 and A5 both credit the Charlotte Observer, but A3 (an Asheville wire) and A4 (with details found in no other report) appear to be independent.

accounts.gist: After an examination before Justice McIlwain, a party of 326 'of both colors' hanged Davis Monday near Heath's store.

framing.detail: The Charlotte Home and Democrat called Davis 'the fiend' and said 'We are glad his request was carried out.'
The Farmer and Mechanic called it 'A terrible affair' and followed it with a warning to parents about 'the prevalence of rape'.
The Daily Gazette ran a short wire under 'Hanged by a Mob', misplacing the lynching in Asheville in its subhead.
The Pickens Sentinel reprinted the Observer under 'Another Ravisher Lynched', describing Davis as 'very black and brutal looking'.
The Anderson Intelligencer gave a plain summary, noting a party 'of both colors'.

conflicts.note: The Observer account of October 18 (A5) is the earliest and most detailed and fixes the hanging on Monday the 17th; the Asheville wire's days appear to be in error.

versions.value: In the charge of a constable and guard, hidden on the way to Monroe jail

conflicts.note: A5 gives the fuller sequence; A2 may be compressing it.
A5 also says a lynching party of 100 was organized first.
A3's own text says Union County; 'Asheville' is the dateline.
Likely an OCR or typesetting difference.
